title: Bernard's Cafe, the camp and Al Capone's tips
summary: He played five and a half years at Michel Bernard's cabaret, once at Capone's camp, and recalls huge tips and Capone's wallet.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: I used to play them numbers. I used to play them numbers like that, going behind all the

man and go to town with them. I mean, all I like that I play. I used to play them numbers like that. I had a good lip in my days. Good lip. I could blow all night, go blow. I blew three days and three nights. What was that? I played all night at the boss's place and go to the camp and play all day for Al Capone. For Al Capone, Al Capone was furnishing my boss with all that liquor. When he was looking for Al Capone in Chicago, Al Capone was right here. Down here. In my place, that's my place where I was playing every night. And my boss had a camp out in the milling body. Knock off, three o'clock in the morning at the cabaret. And we'd take the boot in the yellow cabs and we'd go out to the camp and stay out there and play all day, eat and drink all day. Come right on back to the cabaret. Play that night and go right back to the cabaret. Never changed clothes or nothing. Didn't want us to go home. Man, whoa, brother. That George Gano was playing and the first number he played, he cracked his head. Split. Bam! On the banjo. He said, I'm going home. I said, no. I said, nobody told you to go home. I said, stay now and make this money and buy your head and have some money for you too. Stayed there and had nothing money to buy him six heads. Man, we was making, oh, fifty, seventy-five dollar tip a day. Besides our salary, we was getting paid at night for our nights work, then get paid in the day for our days work and then our tips. Man, well, I never did catch my salary. All the while I worked there. I worked there before they closed him up five years and a half. Before they closed Michelle Bernhardt up. Five years and a half. Never missed a night. I never was a minute late on my job. I don't believe in being late. If you do that for nine o'clock, be there for nine. Quarter to nine, we tune up. Hold the instrument, nine o'clock, we knock the first number. Three o'clock come, we was packing up. Now, I had a very good boss. Michelle was a very reasonable man. He'd give and take. Where was that cabaret? Which? Right here, Frenchman and Gentilly Road. Right after Right after. It's about, just about three minutes to five minutes drive from here. What
was the name of it? Do you remember? Any special name on it or just the boss's name? Oh, it

was, uh, Bernard's, uh, Cafe. That was the name of it. Well, Eddie Victor had it before Michelle Bernard. Michelle Bernard bought it from Eddie Victor. I was playing that for Eddie Victor. And when he came in and he heard the band, behind the place, he was checking every night he'd come around, you know, he heard the band. He asked me would I accept the job. He told me to come out and see him next day. So I went out to his house and saw him. And we got together. We made a nice agreement. Told me, he says, anytime I'll ask you to stay, I'm going to pay you. Don't worry. So when three o'clock would come, he said, August, can you stay till six? I said, okay. We stayed till six. Well, that was extra. We made that extra. And then Al Capone was giving us fifty, seventy, five, hundred dollar tips. Well, he had no limit. And that's the most money I've ever seen one man carry in his pocket. It was Al Capone. He opened his wallet on my bandstand, just like that. He opened his wallet like that, man, and five hundred dollar bills, like that in there. About three inches up the back of three inches. Man, he had his pocket here, was like that with silver. He'd come in and put a half a dollar on every key of the piano, and tell the piano player, play the number now. If you don't knock them on them, put that in your pocket. The piano player was afraid to touch the piano. I said, go ahead and play it, man. Let them fall on the floor, he ain't going to pick them up. I said, knock them all on the floor, we pick them up. Let's see if I can play this number, if I can take it with the glass, this number, what I wrote there. Yeah, I'd like to hear it.
